ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In February 2020, at the International Snowboarding Halfpipe Competition, Chinese athlete Cai Xuetong won the championship. As shown in the figure, the inclination angle of the edge line PQ of the slope is $\theta$. The athlete slides out of the slope at point O on PQ with an initial velocity $v_{0}$, and the direction of the velocity at the moment of sliding out forms an angle $\alpha$ with PQ. After being airborne, the athlete re-enters the slope at point A on PQ. It is known that $\alpha + \theta = 90^{\circ}$, the gravitational acceleration is $g$, and the athlete can be treated as a point mass with air resistance neglected.

1. The distance between points O and A
2. The maximum distance of the athlete from PQ during the leap

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: In February 2020, at the International Snowboarding Halfpipe Competition, Chinese athlete Cai Xuetong won the championship. As shown in the figure, the inclination angle of the edge line PQ of the slope is $\theta$. The athlete slides out of the slope at point O on PQ with an initial velocity $v_{0}$, and the direction of the velocity at the moment of sliding out forms an angle $\alpha$ with PQ. After being airborne, the athlete re-enters the slope at point A on PQ. It is known that $\alpha + \theta = 90^{\circ}$, the gravitational acceleration is $g$, and the athlete can be treated as a point mass with air resistance neglected. 1. The distance between points O and A 2. The maximum distance of the athlete from PQ during the leap
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure, the left part shows the snow halfpipe edge, with the rim labeled by points near O and P and a landing region labeled A. The right schematic shows an inclined straight line PQ sloping downward toward Q. Point O lies on PQ and is the takeoff point; point A also lies on PQ and is the re-entry point. The initial velocity v0 at O is drawn above the inclined line PQ, making angle alpha with PQ. The line PQ makes angle theta with the horizontal, and the airborne path is drawn as a projectile arc from O back to A. Reasoning: Choose the x-axis along PQ downward from O toward A, and the y-axis perpendicular to PQ outward from the slope. Then the initial velocity components are v_x0 = v0 cos alpha, v_y0 = v0 sin alpha. Gravity has component g sin theta along the positive x direction and component g cos theta toward the slope, i.e. negative y direction. Thus x(t) = v0 cos alpha · t + (1/2)g sin theta · t^2, y(t) = v0 sin alpha · t - (1/2)g cos theta · t^2. Because alpha + theta = 90°, we have cos alpha = sin theta and sin alpha = cos theta. For landing back on PQ at A, set y(t)=0 and take the nonzero time: v0 sin alpha · t - (1/2)g cos theta · t^2 = 0, t = 2v0 sin alpha/(g cos theta) = 2v0/g. Then OA = x(t) = v0 cos alpha · (2v0/g) + (1/2)g sin theta · (2v0/g)^2. Using cos alpha = sin theta, OA = 2v0^2 sin theta/g + 2v0^2 sin theta/g = 4v0^2 sin theta/g. For the maximum distance from PQ, maximize y(t). The maximum perpendicular height is y_max = (v0 sin alpha)^2/(2g cos theta). Using sin alpha = cos theta, y_max = v0^2 cos^2 theta/(2g cos theta) = v0^2 cos theta/(2g). Final answer: OA = 4v0^2 sin theta/g; maximum distance from PQ = v0^2 cos theta/(2g).
